title: IBS is real, and it is common
body: Irritable bowel syndrome affects about 1 in 10 people. The gut and the brain are linked by nerves, and in IBS this link becomes over-sensitive, so normal gas and movement are felt as pain or urgency. It does not damage the bowel or turn into cancer.
try: Write down your three most troublesome symptoms. It makes your next doctor's visit far more useful.

title: Eat at the same times every day
body: An irregular eating pattern, with skipped meals followed by large ones, is a common trigger for IBS pain and bloating. The gut settles best with a predictable rhythm.
try: Fix your breakfast, lunch and dinner times for this week and try not to skip any.

title: Keep a two-week symptom diary
body: IBS triggers differ from person to person. A short diary of what you ate, your stress level and your symptoms often shows a pattern that memory alone misses.
try: Start a simple note on your phone today: time, food, symptom and how stressed you felt.

title: Not all fibre suits IBS
body: Soluble fibre, found in oats and isabgol, is gentle and usually helps. Coarse insoluble fibre, such as wheat bran, often makes bloating and pain worse in IBS.
try: If you take bran, try switching to oats or isabgol stirred into plenty of water.

title: Onion and garlic are common triggers
body: Onion and garlic contain fructans, carbohydrates that gut bacteria ferment into gas. They are among the most frequent IBS triggers in Indian cooking.
try: Cook one meal today with less onion and garlic. Pure hing can add flavour, but many hing powders contain wheat, so check the label.

title: Beware of sugar-free sweets
body: Sugar-free gum, mints and sweets often contain sorbitol, mannitol or xylitol. These sweeteners draw water into the gut and cause gas, cramps and loose stools.
try: Check labels for words ending in -itol and avoid them for a week to see if you feel better.

title: Belly breathing calms the gut
body: Stress speeds up or slows down the gut and makes pain feel stronger. Slow breathing from the belly calms the nerves that link the brain and the gut.
try: Breathe in through your nose for 4 counts, letting your belly rise, then out for 6 counts. Do this for 5 minutes.

title: Low-FODMAP is a short plan
body: The low-FODMAP diet helps most people with IBS, but it is meant to be done in stages: a short strict phase, then foods brought back one by one. Staying strict long-term is not needed and can harm gut bacteria.
try: If you want to try it, do it with a doctor or dietitian rather than cutting out foods on your own.

title: Move your body every day
body: Regular physical activity is linked with fewer and milder IBS symptoms, especially bloating and constipation.
try: Take a 20 to 30 minute walk today, or do gentle yoga at home.

title: Go easy on tea and coffee
body: Caffeine stimulates the bowel. For people with diarrhoea-type IBS, several cups a day can bring on urgency and loose motions.
try: Keep to one or two cups a day and notice whether your mornings feel calmer.

title: Large, oily meals bring on cramps
body: Eating stimulates the bowel to contract, and large or fatty meals make this response much stronger. This is why IBS pain often comes soon after a heavy meal.
try: Split today's biggest meal into two smaller ones and choose less fried food.

title: Do not go gluten-free on a guess
body: Wheat can trigger IBS because of its fructans, not always because of gluten. Celiac disease must be tested for while you are still eating wheat, or the test can be falsely normal.
try: If wheat seems to bother you, ask your doctor about a celiac blood test before cutting it out.

title: Choose gentler fruits
body: Apples, pears, mangoes and watermelon contain natural sugars that often cause gas in IBS. Papaya, oranges, kiwi and firm bananas are usually better tolerated.
try: Have one portion of fruit at a time, rather than a large fruit plate.

title: Milk may be the culprit
body: Many people with IBS also digest lactose poorly, which adds to bloating and loose stools. Curd and paneer contain far less lactose than milk.
try: Swap your glass of milk for curd or chaas for a few days and see if bloating eases.

title: Signs that are not IBS
body: IBS does not cause blood in the stool, weight loss, fever, anaemia or symptoms that wake you at night. These need proper tests.
try: If you have any of these, or your symptoms started after age 45, book a check-up rather than treating it as IBS.

title: Make dal and rajma easier to digest
body: Legumes are healthy but contain carbohydrates that ferment into gas. Soaking and thorough cooking reduce the problem, and small portions are better tolerated.
try: Soak legumes overnight, discard the water, pressure-cook well, and keep to a small bowl.

title: Eat slowly, swallow less air
body: Eating fast, talking while eating, and drinking through straws make you swallow air, which adds to bloating.
try: Put your spoon down between bites today and take at least 15 minutes over lunch.

title: Skip the fizzy drinks
body: Soft drinks and soda put gas straight into the gut, and many also contain sweeteners that trigger IBS.
try: Swap fizzy drinks for plain water, nimbu pani without sugar, or chaas.

title: IBS with constipation
body: For constipation-type IBS, soluble fibre, enough water and a regular toilet routine help more than strong laxatives taken now and then.
try: Sit on the toilet after breakfast with your feet on a small stool, and drink a glass of water first.

title: IBS with loose motions
body: For diarrhoea-type IBS, smaller meals, fewer trigger foods and less caffeine often reduce urgency. Effective medicines are also available.
try: Note what you ate before your last bad day. If urgency affects your work or travel, ask your doctor about treatment.

title: Probiotics: try, then review
body: Some people with IBS feel better on a probiotic, but results vary between products and people.
try: If you try one, stick to a single product for up to 12 weeks, then stop it if you notice no benefit.

title: Sleep affects your gut
body: Poor or short sleep is linked with worse IBS pain and bloating the next day.
try: Keep a fixed bedtime this week and put your phone away 30 minutes before sleep.

title: Warmth for cramps
body: A warm water bottle or heating pad on the belly relaxes the gut muscles and can ease cramping pain.
try: Keep a hot water bottle ready for the next time cramps start.

title: Peppermint oil can help
body: Peppermint oil capsules relax the gut muscles and reduce IBS pain in many people. They can worsen heartburn in some.
try: Ask your doctor whether enteric-coated peppermint oil capsules suit you.

title: IBS and periods
body: Many women notice IBS symptoms get worse just before and during their periods because of hormone changes.
try: Mark your cycle in your symptom diary and plan lighter, regular meals in those days.

title: Do not cut out too much
body: Removing many foods at once can leave you short of fibre, calcium and other nutrients, and can make eating stressful.
try: Remove only one suspected trigger at a time, for two weeks, before deciding.

title: Gut-focused therapy works
body: Cognitive behavioural therapy and gut-directed hypnotherapy calm the gut-brain link and have strong evidence for IBS, especially when diet changes are not enough.
try: If stress clearly drives your symptoms, ask your doctor about these treatments.

title: Travelling with IBS
body: Changes in routine, meal timing and water during travel commonly trigger flare-ups.
try: Carry familiar safe snacks and water, and keep your meal times as close to normal as you can.

title: Festival eating with IBS
body: Festive meals combine many triggers at once: rich food, sweets, onion and garlic, late meals and less sleep.
try: Enjoy small portions of your favourites, eat at regular times, and take a short walk after meals.

title: IBS can be controlled
body: There is no single cure, but most people improve a lot with the right mix of diet, routine, stress care and, when needed, medicines.
try: If IBS still affects your daily life, book a review. A tailored plan works better than trial and error.

title: Indian foods that are gentler on IBS
body: Low-FODMAP foods are fermented less by gut bacteria, so they make less gas. In an Indian kitchen these include rice, poha, oats, potato, carrot, tomato, spinach, brinjal, cucumber, paneer and small portions of moong dal. Wheat, onion, garlic, rajma, chana, cauliflower and mushrooms are higher in FODMAPs.
try: For one meal today, build your plate from the gentler list and note how your gut feels afterwards.

title: Worry turns up the pain
body: When you are always watching for the next cramp, the brain turns up the volume on normal gut signals. Fear of symptoms can itself make pain and urgency worse.
try: When a familiar IBS cramp starts, remind yourself that it is uncomfortable but not dangerous, breathe slowly, and carry on with what you were doing.

title: IBS can start after food poisoning
body: About 1 in 10 people develop IBS after a bout of gastroenteritis, even once the infection itself has cleared. This is called post-infectious IBS, and it often improves slowly over months.
try: If pain or loose motions have lasted several weeks after a stomach infection, see a doctor for a check-up instead of taking repeated courses of antibiotics.

title: Kiwi for constipation-type IBS
body: Studies show that eating two green kiwis a day can soften stools and make bowel movements more regular. Kiwi is also low in FODMAPs, so it is usually well tolerated in IBS.
try: Have two kiwis today, and keep it up daily for four weeks to judge whether it helps.

title: Loose motions after gallbladder removal
body: Some people get watery diarrhoea after the gallbladder is removed, or have IBS-like loose motions that do not settle. In some of them, extra bile acids reaching the colon are the cause, and this is treated differently from IBS.
try: If your loose motions started after gallbladder surgery, or have not improved with usual IBS care, ask your doctor about bile acid diarrhoea.

title: Keeping IBS calm through the Chhath fast
body: Long fasts, especially without water, can harden stools in constipation-type IBS. A large meal at the end of a fast can bring on cramps and urgency in diarrhoea-type IBS.
try: If you are fasting for Chhath, drink plenty of water in the days before and break the fast with a small portion of familiar food. If you have diabetes or another illness, check with your doctor before fasting without water.

title: Do not sit and strain
body: A feeling that the bowel has not emptied fully is common in IBS, even when it has. Straining or sitting for a long time to pass more stool can lead to piles and fissures.
try: Keep toilet time to about 5 minutes, leave your phone outside, and get up once you have passed stool even if that feeling remains.

title: Winter and constipation-type IBS
body: In cold weather most of us feel less thirsty and move around less. For people with constipation-type IBS, this often means harder stools, more straining and more bloating.
try: Keep a bottle of water at your desk and finish it by evening. Warm water and clear soups count too, and a short indoor walk after meals helps.

title: FODMAPs add up across a meal
body: Many trigger foods are fine in small amounts. Trouble starts when several of them come together in one meal. Chole with lots of onion and garlic, wheat bhature and a sweet lassi at one sitting is a heavy FODMAP load.
try: Keep only one higher-FODMAP food on your plate at a time, and pair it with gentler foods such as rice, carrot, cucumber or spinach.

title: Thyroid problems can mimic IBS
body: An overactive thyroid can cause frequent loose motions, and an underactive one can cause constipation and bloating. Both are common, especially in women, and a simple blood test picks them up.
try: If your bowel habit has changed and you have not had a thyroid test in the past year, ask your doctor whether you need one.

title: Unhurried mornings for loose-motion IBS
body: Rushing, and worrying about the journey ahead, can bring on urgency before you even leave home. A calm start gives the gut time to settle after the normal morning bowel movement.
try: Wake up 20 minutes earlier tomorrow, have breakfast sitting down, and allow time for the toilet before you leave.

title: Chillies can bring on urgency
body: Chillies contain capsaicin, which acts on pain nerves in the gut. In some people with IBS, especially the diarrhoea type, a very spicy meal brings on burning pain and urgency within hours.
try: Keep the chilli mild today and flavour your food with jeera, ajwain, ginger or fresh coriander.

title: Alcohol often worsens IBS
body: Alcohol irritates the gut lining and speeds up the bowel, so loose motions and cramps are common the next morning. Beer and sweet mixers also add gas and fermentable sugars.
try: If you drink, keep several alcohol-free days each week, never drink on an empty stomach, and note in your diary how your gut feels the next day.

title: New, constant bloating needs a check
body: IBS bloating usually comes and goes, often building up by evening and easing after sleep. Bloating that is there almost every day and keeps getting worse, especially in women over 50, can come from the ovaries or from fluid in the belly.
try: See a doctor if your bloating is new, has been constant for more than three weeks, or comes with feeling full quickly, weight loss or a change in urine habit.

title: Wheat roti and IBS bloating
body: Wheat contains fructans, a FODMAP that gut bacteria ferment into gas, which can cause bloating in IBS. This is different from celiac disease, and most people only need to cut down on wheat.
try: If roti seems to bloat you, swap one roti at dinner for plain rice or a jowar or ragi roti for a week, and note how your belly feels.

title: Know your IBS type from your stool
body: IBS is grouped by the usual form of your stool: mostly hard (constipation type), mostly loose (diarrhoea type) or a mix of both. The type decides which diet changes and treatments are likely to help, and it can change over the years.
try: For one week, note the form of each stool, from hard lumps to watery, and show this record at your next doctor's visit.

title: Choose gentler nuts for IBS
body: Cashews and pistachios are high in FODMAPs and often bring on gas in IBS. Peanuts, walnuts and a small number of almonds are usually much better tolerated.
try: If you snack on nuts, have a small handful of roasted peanuts or walnuts today in place of cashews.

title: Crowded gatherings and IBS urgency
body: Gurpurab on 24 November and the wedding season bring long gatherings, and worrying about finding a toilet can itself set off cramps and urgency. Knowing where the toilet is calms this gut-brain loop and often eases the urge.
try: When you arrive at the gurdwara, a wedding or any crowded place today, find the nearest toilet first, then settle in and enjoy the day.

title: A stool test can rule out colitis
body: Ongoing loose motions can come from inflammatory bowel disease such as ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease, and not only from IBS. A simple stool test called faecal calprotectin helps your doctor tell the two apart and decide whether a colonoscopy is needed.
try: If you have diarrhoea-type symptoms and have never had this test, ask your doctor about it. See a doctor soon if you notice blood in the stool, loose motions that wake you at night, weight loss or fever.

title: Split dals are gentler than whole ones
body: Whole rajma, chhole and kala chana are high in FODMAPs called GOS, which ferment in the gut and make gas. Husked split dals such as dhuli moong and masoor usually cause less gas and still give good protein.
try: On a day your belly feels unsettled, make dhuli moong or masoor dal in place of rajma or chhole, and keep it to one katori.

title: Do not let IBS shrink your life
body: Many people with IBS slowly stop going out, travelling or eating with others for fear of symptoms. This avoidance keeps the worry high, and the worry in turn makes the gut more sensitive.
try: Pick one small thing you have been avoiding, like a short outing or a meal with friends, and do it this week with a simple plan in place.
